scene: Second dose of succinylcholine for laryngospasm. HR drops to 38.
question: Most likely cause?
why: Succinylcholine is two acetylcholine molecules joined together, so it also stimulates cardiac muscarinic receptors. Bradycardia is more likely with a repeat dose and in children. Treat with atropine.
pearl: Giving a second dose? Have atropine drawn up first.
caption:
Second dose of succinylcholine for laryngospasm, and the heart rate drops to 38. Why? 💉

Comment your pick before the answer 👇

Succinylcholine is two acetylcholine molecules joined together, so it doesn't just hit the neuromuscular junction: it stimulates cardiac muscarinic receptors too. Bradycardia is more likely with a repeat dose and in children. Atropine is the fix, and many clinicians have it ready before re-dosing.

slides.title: Neostigmine or sugammadex?
slides.sub: How each reversal agent works, and when it falls short.

slides.body: It inhibits acetylcholinesterase so acetylcholine can outcompete the relaxant. It has a ceiling: it can't reverse deep block.

bullets: Time: full effect takes about 10 minutes
No effect on cisatracurium or succinylcholine
Dose depends on depth of block

slides.body: Reversal is not the endpoint. Confirm a TOF ratio of 0.9 or more with quantitative monitoring before extubation.
slides.pearl: Residual block hides behind a strong hand grip.

slides.title: Reverse it. Then measure it.
slides.body: Know which agent fits the block in front of you.

caption:
Neostigmine or sugammadex: do you know why one can't reverse a deep block? 💊

Swipe for the essentials: neostigmine boosts acetylcholine and has a ceiling → why it needs some recovery first and glycopyrrolate alongside → how sugammadex encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium (but not cisatracurium or succinylcholine) → why quantitative TOF still decides when the tube comes out.

💡 Sugammadex can reduce the effect of hormonal contraceptives. Counsel patients per your institution's policy.

scene: 82-year-old, steady sevo, quiet part of the case. EEG shows burst suppression.
question: Next move?
why: Older brains need less anesthetic for the same effect. If the patient is stable and stimulation allows, reduce the volatile and recheck the EEG. Also rule out low blood pressure as a cause.
pearl: Burst suppression in older adults is linked to postoperative delirium.
caption:
82 years old, steady sevo, quiet part of the case, and the EEG is in burst suppression. What's your move? 🧠

Comment your pick before the answer 👇

Older brains need less anesthetic for the same effect. If the patient is stable and the surgical stimulus allows, lighten the anesthetic and watch the raw EEG recover. Check the blood pressure too: hypoperfusion can suppress the EEG. Burst suppression in older adults is linked to postoperative delirium.

scene: Preeclampsia, uterine atony after delivery. Oxytocin is already running.
question: Which one do you avoid?
why: Methylergonovine is a potent vasoconstrictor and can cause severe hypertension, so it's avoided in preeclampsia and chronic hypertension. Carboprost is the one to avoid in asthma.
pearl: Ergot for atony? Check the blood pressure first.
caption:
Preeclampsia, BP 168/108, and the uterus won't contract after delivery. Which uterotonic stays in the drawer? 🤰

Comment your pick before the answer 👇

Methylergonovine is a potent vasoconstrictor that can spike the blood pressure, so it's avoided in preeclampsia and chronic hypertension. Carboprost is the one to avoid in asthma because it can trigger bronchospasm. Know the contraindication for each before the hemorrhage starts.

slides.title: Preoxygenation buys you time. Do it right.
slides.sub: Fill the lungs with oxygen before the apnea starts.

slides.body: You're replacing nitrogen in the functional residual capacity with oxygen. The FRC is the reservoir that keeps SpO2 up during apnea.

bullets: 100% O2 at high fresh gas flow

slides.pearl: Head up 20-25 degrees helps the FRC in obese patients.

slides.title: Seal. Flow. Time.
slides.body: Watch the end-tidal O2, not the clock.

caption:
Three minutes on the mask: is that enough preoxygenation? Watch the end-tidal O2, not the clock. 🫁

Swipe for the essentials: target an end-tidal O2 of 0.9 or more → tight seal, high flow, tidal breathing or 8 deep breaths → who desaturates fastest → head-up positioning, CPAP and nasal oxygen to stretch your safe apnea time.

💡 A mask leak lets room air in. No seal, no reservoir.

scene: Trauma, massive transfusion. Ten units in, BP falling, QT lengthening.
question: What's low?
why: Citrate in stored blood binds calcium, and the liver can't clear it fast enough in shock. Low ionized calcium weakens contraction, lowers vascular tone and worsens coagulopathy. Check it early and replace it.
pearl: In massive transfusion, check ionized calcium early and often.
caption:
Ten units into a massive transfusion: BP falling, QT stretching out. What's quietly dropping? 🩸

Comment your pick before the answer 👇

Citrate in stored blood binds calcium, and a shocked liver can't clear it fast enough. Low ionized calcium weakens the heart, drops vascular tone and makes coagulopathy worse. Check it early, check it often, and replace it per your massive transfusion protocol.
